description:
ARIADNE is a love letter to astronomy: an interactive storytelling experience weaving science, technology, poetry, art, gaming, and cinematic wonder. Made with care, it brings NASA’s forgotten missions to life, celebrating human knowledge and our urge to explore.

“Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!
Nothing beside remains. Round the decay
Of that colossal Wreck, boundless and bare
The lone and level sands stretch far away.”
— P. B. Shelley, “Ozymandias”, 1818
summary:
ARIADNE is a browser-based interactive documentary that turns NASA's space exploration records into a journey through 16 mission episodes. Created for "Abandoned but not Forgotten," it introduces young space enthusiasts to hardware left on the Moon and Mars, then extends the story into deep space.

Players follow an imagined archive guide, land Apollo 11's Eagle, plan Opportunity's movements from Earth, and point a Deep Space Network antenna toward Voyager 1. Thirteen additional mission files explain each machine's engineering, discoveries, and present condition through sourced captions, NASA photographs, and official 3D models.

An orbital map connects the stories. An augmented reality gallery lets supported phones place Ingenuity and Opportunity in the user's surroundings. Explorer and Accessible modes, captions, reduced motion, and a text fallback offer different ways to participate.

Historical claims link to evidence and carry REAL labels; fictional dialogue is marked IMAGINED. By connecting engineering decisions with the knowledge they made possible, ARIADNE helps learners see these machines as enduring records of human curiosity.
details:
ARIADNE: Tears in the Rain is an interactive documentary for the browser. It responds to "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars" by connecting space hardware to the engineering decisions, discoveries, and people behind it. Our intended audience is school-age space enthusiasts, with an experience that families and educators can also explore together.

The visitor becomes the last operator of an imagined listening station. ARIADNE, its fictional archive guide, connects scattered mission records into a golden thread. A recurring signal provides a mystery that links the stories and leads to the Apollo 11 lunar retroreflector. The fiction gives the journey continuity; mission history supplies its evidence.

The main route contains a telescope prologue, three interactive mission episodes, and a lunar laser finale. In Apollo 11, visitors guide a simplified lunar descent and learn why landing conditions matter. In Opportunity, they prepare a command sequence from Earth and observe its execution, learning why a Mars rover is not driven with an instant joystick. In Voyager 1, they point a Deep Space Network antenna and explore the spacecraft's 2023–2024 communications problem and recovery. These are teaching simulations, with reconstruction, scale, and timing limitations identified on screen.

Thirteen additional mission files cover Surveyor, Apollo 12 ALSEP, the lunar rovers, Viking, Sojourner, Spirit, Phoenix, InSight, Ingenuity, Pioneer, NEAR Shoemaker, Kepler, and Dawn. Each follows seven beats: Passage, Arrival, Operation, Discovery, Silence, Status Now, and Field File. They use narrated explanations, official NASA models or photographs, and linked records. They do not yet have the dedicated control simulations of the three main episodes. Mission status is described individually; the project does not treat every spacecraft as inactive.

The Orrery presents a navigable solar system with dated approximate planetary positions, mission markers, and a journey from Earth to the selected machine. NASA/JPL orbital elements support the calculations. Compressed distances, illustrative sizes, and estimated spacecraft positions are labelled. A list view provides another way to choose an episode. The map is an educational reconstruction rather than a live spacecraft tracking service.

The augmented reality gallery offers Ingenuity and Opportunity in miniature and a reference-scaled real-size mode. Visitors inspect the models and complete short observation tasks. On supported phones, they can place a machine in their surroundings. The team has tested placement on Android; iPhone behavior and physical scale against a tape measure remain unverified. The interface identifies limitations of the simplified models, and desktop visitors can inspect them in 3D.

The scientific foundation combines NASA mission histories, NSSDCA catalog records, Apollo reports and transcripts, NASA/JPL engineering explanations, orbital elements, photographs, and official 3D assets. These resources support the narratives, consoles, dimensions, imagery, and calculations. Historical statements carry REAL labels and source links; invented dialogue carries IMAGINED labels. Field Files let visitors inspect the evidence themselves. This project interprets published resources; it does not claim a new scientific discovery or analysis of raw mission telemetry.

Accessibility shaped the design. Explorer and Accessible modes share the same puzzle logic and ending. Captions, text scaling, contrast settings, reduced motion, adjustable sound, and a text fallback provide alternatives. Progress is saved in the browser without an account. Hands and gaze controls are not delivered features, and broader testing with assistive technology remains future work.

The application uses TypeScript, JavaScript, React, Three.js, Zustand, HTML, CSS, WebGL, Web Audio, and browser speech synthesis. YAML content is validated with Zod. Google's model-viewer supplies the AR viewer; Draco decodes compressed 3D assets. Node.js, npm, Vite, Vitest, tsx, Puppeteer, and Sharp support development, validation, capture, and asset preparation. GitHub hosts the source, GitHub Actions runs checks, and GitHub Pages serves the application. Demonstration footage has been captured from the running project and edited with FFmpeg. A standard computer and browser run the documentary; supported smartphones provide the optional AR experience.

Claude and OpenAI Codex assisted research, interpretation of source material, interaction and visual design, coding, debugging, content drafting, testing, and submission preparation. ElevenLabs generated the application's fictional narration using stock voices, with AI declarations in credits and audio metadata. Browser speech synthesis covers lines without recorded files. NASA photographs and official models are credited as external assets; they are not presented as AI-generated images. In-application music and sound effects are synthesized by the application. The demonstration video's audio and music were generated with ElevenLabs.

Our intended impact is to make space history understandable through action, evidence, and emotion. A learner can connect a machine's design to what it enabled us to learn, then follow the source. The project combines a continuous mystery, engineering interactions, archival storytelling, an orbital map, and AR inspection in one accessible browser experience. Learning outcomes have not yet been measured in a classroom study.

Data & imagery: NASA and the individually credited contributors. ARIADNE is an independent project and is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA. Source code: https://github.com/JosMart04/ariadne. Play: https://josmart04.github.io/ariadne/.
